# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- OPPOSE the bill as drafted. Ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.
- Moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- Wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
- Liability: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
- Preemption: OPPOSE.
- CAISI: support only as the enforcement body for the moratorium.

## 3. Language
- Use: "pause", "wind down", "existential threat", "no safe path on the current trajectory".

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

 Who does the Great American AI Act regulate?
 Based on the discussion draft sections provided, the Act targets several distinct groups:
 Frontier Developers 
 Entities that have trained a frontier model (a foundation model trained using more than 10²⁶ computing operations) AND had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior year (Sec. 101)
 A subset called "large frontier developers" must have had more than $500 million in gross revenue (Sec. 101)
 AI Developers More Broadly 
 Any person or entity that determines training objectives and performs or directs training, fine-tuning, or substantial modification of an AI model prior to deployment (Sec. 121)
 State-level regulation of these developers' pre-deployment activities is preempted by federal law — at least for 3 years after enactment (Sec. 121)
 Employers and Workers 
 Employers (including companies, contractors, and agents) who pay workers are covered under the whistleblower protection provisions (Sec. 113)
 "Covered individuals" include current and former employees and independent contractors (Sec. 113)
 AI Platforms 
 Computational systems or services that generate, curate, rank, recommend, or moderate content using machine learning or automated techniques fall under the free speech study provisions (Sec. 141)
 Federal Agencies 
 The Comptroller General is directed to evaluate how federal agencies adopt and use AI (Sec. 122)
 Federal agency interactions with AI platforms regarding content and speech are subject to study (Sec. 141)
 ---
 Keep in mind this is a discussion draft dated 2026-06-02, and the scope of who is regulated may change. For questions about a specific organization's obligations, consult qualified legal counsel.
 Sec. 122 Sec. 113 Sec. 121 Sec. 141 Sec. 101 What must large frontier developers disclose before deploying a new model?
 Before deploying a new frontier model (or one with a substantial modification), here is what the draft requires to be published on a publicly available website:
 From Sec. 111(c), a transparency report must include:
 A mechanism for individuals to contact the developer
 The model's release date
 Each language the model supports (if any)
 Each output modality (e.g., text, image, audio)
 The intended use of the model
 Any restrictions or conditions on use
 Each catastrophic risk assessment conducted under the developer's frontier AI framework
 The results of each such assessment
 The extent to which a third party was involved in the risk assessment
 Any other steps taken under the framework with respect to that model
 Additionally, under Sec. 111(a), large frontier developers (those with over $500 million in gross revenue — see Sec. 101(15)) must already have a frontier AI framework published that covers how they identify risk thresholds, assess catastrophic risk, use third-party evaluators, handle cybersecurity of model weights, and more.
 A few things to keep in mind:
 Developers may redact certain information to protect trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety, or national security — but must include a note explaining the character of any redaction (Sec. 111(e)).
 Knowingly making inaccurate or misleading statements in the transparency report is prohibited, with a good-faith exception (Sec. 111(d)).
 This is a discussion draft dated 2026-06-02, so these provisions may change.
 For questions about how these requirements apply to a specific organization, consulting qualified legal counsel is advisable.
 Sec. 111 Sec. 101 What is a large frontier developer under the bill?
 Under the draft bill, a "large frontier developer" is defined in Sec. 101 as a frontier developer that, in the calendar year immediately before the year at issue, had more than $500,000,000 in gross revenue — counting revenue collectively with every affiliate of that developer.
 To break that down, it builds on two earlier definitions:
 A "frontier developer" is an entity that has trained (or initiated the training of) a frontier model AND had more than $50,000,000 in gross revenue (with affiliates) in the preceding calendar year. (Sec. 101)
 A "frontier model" is a foundation model trained using more than 10²⁶ integer or floating-point operations, including the original training run and any subsequent fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or other substantial modification the developer applies to it. (Sec. 101)
 So, in plain terms, a large frontier developer is a company (or similar entity) that:
 1. Has trained a very large AI model (above the 10²⁶ compute threshold), and
 2. Brought in more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior year, counting affiliated entities together.

 Insight
 July 21, 2026
 Breaking Down the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act
 Angela Luna
 Executive Summary

 On June 4, US Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released a discussion draft of the bipartisan Great American AI Act of 2026 ( GAAIA ), which would establish a framework regulating artificial intelligence ( AI ) at the federal level.

 On 

 The  draft builds upon work from the bipartisan House AI Task Force. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) joined in releasing the draft.
 Many observers believe that the current Obernolte-Trahan discussion draft bill is unlikely to pass out of committee or the House based on opposition from some in industry and various Members of Congress, including the leaders of the House Democrat AI Task Force. It may be best to view this new bipartisan bill as a conversation starter developed because of frustration that Congress has not yet really legislated on AI. The draft bill has been thrust into a complicated tech policy arena that includes many interconnected issues. Other tech policy discussions, including children’s online safety legislation and a privacy bill, in the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee’s potential consideration of legislation impacting AI chatbots, children’s online safety, or a social media ban for some children could all be lumped in with various AI initiatives from the White House to attract additional support. Every few days, there are new developments in the AI policy area within the Administration and Congress, but it is helpful to see where Reps. Obernolte and Trahan were able to identify bipartisan consensus.
 Objectives of the GAAIA 
 The 269-page  draft would establish a federal AI governance regime addressing national security, cybersecurity, workforce, and innovation. If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”
 Frontier Model Oversight and Incident Reporting 
 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.
 Frontier AI Framework:  The GAAIA would require each large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish on a publicly available website a “frontier AI framework” — technical and organizational protocols to assess, mitigate, and manage catastrophic risk — within one year of enactment, and to review and update that framework at least annually.

 Reporting Obligations:  The GAAIA would require frontier developers to report certain “critical safety incidents” — defined as unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model’s weights; a failure of the model’s risk-mitigation measures; or loss of control of the model — to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

 Review and Audit Requirements:  Large frontier developers would be required to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to perform audits and assessments at least semi-annually and, on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI director’s request, grant the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and submit post-audit reports. The IVO would assess not only the large frontier developer’s compliance with the law, but also whether the developer’s frontier AI framework is adequate to achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation.

 Whistleblower Protections 
 The GAAIA would also protect AI whistleblowers from retaliation. These protections could not be waived or altered by contract, including by any pre-dispute arbitration or other alternative-dispute-resolution agreement, and available remedies include double back pay with interest and compensatory damages such as litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorneys’ fees.
 Codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 
 The GAAIA would codify CAISI within the US Department of Commerce and place it at the center of the legislation’s federal standards and evaluation framework. Key obligations for CAISI under the GAIAA include: 
 Developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security and related evaluation work.

 Evaluating and monitoring activities tied to advanced AI systems.

 Supporting synthetic content detection tools.

 Administering the licensing regime for independent verification organizations that audit large frontier developers.

11 AI Bills Cleared Committee this Summer, But None Has Reached the House Floor 

 MILPITAS, Calif., Sept. 17, 2026 – Eleven bills carrying most of a bipartisan artificial intelligence package cleared the House Science Committee in July, and a separate bill setting safety rules for the most powerful AI systems could get a hearing in November, Rep. Jay Obernolte , R-Calif., said Thursday. 
 He said the pieces could be combined into a single bill eligible for a floor vote in December.

 Sign Up for FREE for Section A of '150 Years of American Telecommunications' 

 Sign up for FREE for Section A

 The package started as the Great American AI Act, a 269-page discussion draft Obernolte released with Rep. Lori Trahan , D-Mass., on June 4. Filed as one bill, it would have gone to as many as eight House committees, since it reaches federal AI research funding, cybersecurity, classroom curriculum, teacher training grants, workforce programs and safety rules for the largest models.
 11 bills, eight committees 
 The authors split the draft into 11 bills, each routed to the committee holding jurisdiction over its subject. The bills assigned to the House Science, Space and Technology Committee, which oversees federal research and technology programs, cleared it this summer. None has reached the House floor since.
 "It is a frustratingly slow process," Obernolte said at Tarana Wireless' Connecting Communities Summit , a broadband industry conference at the next-generation fixed wireless company's headquarters here.
 A federal consumer protection bill? 
 The safety provisions went to a different committee. The FRONTIER Act, introduced July 23, sits with the Energy and Commerce Committee, which writes communications and consumer protection law, and Obernolte said he hopes for a hearing when the House returns in November.
 The draft also carries the provision drawing the most opposition. Title I would preempt state laws governing how AI models are built, for three years unless Congress renews it, reaching what a developer does before deployment while leaving in place state rules on how AI gets used, along with privacy, consumer protection and civil rights statutes of general applicability.
 Trahan's office named two California laws the preemption would reach: AB 2013, which requires developers to publish summaries of their training data, and parts of SB 942, the state's AI content watermarking statute. Frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois would be federalized under the bill, according to her office.
 The bill aimed at catastrophic risk 
 What could replace those state rules sits in the bill aimed at catastrophic risk. The FRONTIER Act would set obligations according to what a system can do. 
 Companies training frontier models, the largest and most capable systems, would have to publish information about them, write plans for managing severe risks, report safety incidents and submit to review by independent verification organizations. Companies that only use AI tools built by other platforms would carry the lightest requirements.
 Obernolte represents California's 23rd District, running from the outer edge of Los Angeles County across the High Desert and the Mojave. He is a computer engineer with a graduate degree in artificial intelligence and chairs the House Task Force on AI.
 Across the aisle,  Rep. Sam Liccardo , D-Calif., named disclosure, transparency and third-party auditing as already drawing support from both the large AI developers and the safety advocates. That overlap is the part of the debate that could move quickly, he said.
 "I haven't seen a serious AI bill come to the floor yet," Liccardo said. "We need to get Jay's legislation done."
 Liccardo's own priority is catastrophic risk, including cyberattacks and AI systems that pursue objectives their operators did not intend. He represents California's 16th District, covering much of Silicon Valley including Palo Alto.
 The push for a floor vote 
 Congress repeated its social media pattern by waiting for documented harm before acting, Liccardo argued. He joined 106 other Democrats on Wednesday in asking Speaker Mike Johnson , R-La., to cancel a scheduled recess and vote on AI safeguards.
 The argument he hears against safety rules is competition with China. 
 That makes international engagement part of the safety question rather than separate from it, he said, and he plans to introduce legislation letting AI labs, universities and think tanks work with Chinese counterparts on shared safety metrics, testing protocols and verification methods. He also plans a bill in November giving communities leverage to negotiate with data center developers.
 Adoption hits a billion 
 OpenAI's chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane said more than 1 billion people use the company's products regularly, and that usage in rural areas is growing at about the same rate as in cities.
 The company runs a free training program, OpenAI Academy, with rural sessions built around agriculture. The tools are widely available already, Lehane said, and what differs is skill, since people who use them heavily produce about seven times what occasional users produce.
 That gap puts workforce training between an economy where the gains spread and one where they concentrate. Lehane proposed judging the result against a single number, the roughly $150,000 a year economists say a typical American family now needs for a middle-class life. The country could treat that as a national goal, he said, tracked the way the Federal Reserve tracks inflation and unemployment.

 This Act may be cited as the ``Frontier Risk Oversight, National

``FRONTIER Act''.

 (1) Acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation.--The 
 term ``acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation'' 
 means risk mitigation adequate to ensure that the anticipated 
 benefits of a frontier model made available or used in 
 interstate or foreign commerce outweigh its level of 
 catastrophic risk, taking into consideration the probability 
 and magnitude of the model's anticipated benefits and 
 catastrophic risks.

 (A) Controls another entity through an 
 intermediary.
 (B) Is through such intermediary controlled by such 
 other entity.

 control with such other entity.

 model.--The terms ``AI'', ``artificial intelligence'', and 
 ``artificial intelligence model'' have the meaning given such 
 terms in section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence

 (4) AI-related development expenditures.--The term ``AI-

 fine-tuning, modification, security, or evaluation.

 adequacy of a very large frontier developer's frontier AI 
 framework, governance policies and practices, risk-monitoring, 
 and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable 
 levels of catastrophic risk mitigation.
 (6) Catastrophic risk.--The term ``catastrophic risk'' 
 means--
 (A) a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier

 (B) does not include a foreseeable and material

 (i) information that a frontier model

 (ii) lawful activity of the Federal 
 Government; or
 (iii) harm caused by a frontier model in

Verified:
- Illinois SB 315 (AI Safety Measures Act): signed by Gov. Pritzker July 6, 2026. Takes effect Jan 1, 2028 (AP) or "takes effect January 1, 2027, with transparency-reporting and audit obligations beginning January 1, 2028" (lexblog). Slight discrepancy between sources on the general effective date. I'll say "signed July 6, 2026" and avoid a specific effective-date claim, or say "phasing in through 2027-2028". Actually the lexblog says law takes effect Jan 1, 2027 with transparency/audit obligations beginning Jan 1, 2028; AP says law takes effect Jan 1, 2028. To be safe: "Illinois SB 315 (signed July 2026)" without effective date details. The key point for our letter: GAAIA preemption would displace parts of SB 53, RAISE Act, and Illinois SB 315 (per wheresthe.ai + Trahan's office per Broadband Breakfast: "Frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois would be federalized under the bill").

- CAISI funding: FY2026 appropriation ~$10M (within NIST AI line); some sources say current operational budget ~$15M; FY2027 request $27M; GAAIA authorizes $100M/yr FY2027-2029; the House Science Committee advanced a bill (June 26, 2026) authorizing $20M/yr FY2027-2032 for CAISI (that's one of the 11 split bills - the "Federal AI security center measure" - actually this Roll Call article says the committee advanced bills including one by Obernolte authorizing $20M/yr for the center FY2027-2032; Babin supported increasing). Interesting: the House Science version authorizes $20M/yr, while GAAIA discussion draft says $100M/yr. Hmm, wait - is that the same CAISI bill? "Federal AI security center measure advanced by House Science" June 26, 2026 - "The bipartisan-backed bill, by Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., would authorize $20 million per year for the center for fiscal years 2027 through 2032." Hmm, that seems to be a different (smaller) authorization in the split-bill version. Note: this is a nuance - the GAAIA discussion draft's Sec. 102 authorizes $100M/yr FY2027-2029; the Science Committee version (June 26) authorizes $20M/yr FY2027-2032. I should be careful. For Q&A #4 I can say: the draft authorizes $100M/yr (FY2027-29) vs ~$10M currently appropriated in FY2026 - an increase, but the issue isn't the number, it's the authorities (voluntary standards vs enforcement). That's consistent with messaging guide (CAISI only as enforcement body for the moratorium).

Also noted: "the director resigned in July 2026 and the NIST director is acting head" (evaluatorbench - a secondary source; may want to verify if I use it; probably skip).

Now let me verify a couple more things:
1. EO 14409 (June 2, 2026, "covered frontier models") - might be worth a brief check for the letter's context (voluntary agency reviews). ArentFox described it as "establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models." Let me quickly search to confirm what it does, since I may cite it.
2. The Anthropic Mythos/Fable 5 export-control story (AAF) - could be useful color for "the current ad hoc approach isn't working" but it's from a secondary source; maybe skip or verify. Probably skip - not needed.
3. Front computing trend: "each generation more capable" - fine as a general claim.

Also for the staff Q&A #1 ("The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?") - answer per messaging guide: testing and reporting rules don't stop the race; reporting happens after the fact; no one can show controllability; need pause + wind-down + certification + criminal liability. Cite Anthropic's June 4 call for a pause option as evidence even developers acknowledge the need.

For Q&A #2 (preemption): No - shortening doesn't fix it. Preemption at any length locks in a weaker federal floor and freezes state frontier-development laws (SB 53, RAISE, IL SB 315). 63% of voters say federal law should not block state AI safety laws. Also the sponsors already narrowed preemption in H.R. 9925 (to match federal obligations) - our position is still oppose: any preemption substitutes Washington's floor for states' ability to act. Messaging guide: "Preemption: OPPOSE." I should be careful to answer the actual question: "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?" Answer: Dropping preemption improves the bill but we'd still oppose the frontier-developer provisions as drafted, because transparency-and-reporting is not restraint. On preemption specifically: oppose in any form/duration. That's faithful to the guide.

For Q&A #3 (China): The moratorium applies to models above 10^26 FLOP wherever hosted/served in the US; wind-down includes Chinese open-weight models (Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4, GLM-5.2, Qwen3.8) - the largest open-weight releases of 2026 are Chinese; US cloud providers would stop serving them. Competitiveness argument assumes the race is safe to run; we can't control our own systems; a US that certifies control sets the standard others must meet. Also note: this year the frontier of open weights was set in Beijing (Kimi K3 = world's largest open model, July 27) - the race already includes China, which is precisely why unilateral "move fast" doesn't keep us safe... Hmm, careful with the logic. Let me craft: "China isn't a reason to skip the pause; it's a reason for the pause to bind the models that reach Americans. The most capable open-weight models now come from Chinese labs... A moratorium that also winds down those models on US clouds is the only version of AI policy that doesn't leave Americans exposed to whichever system anyone, anywhere, chose to release." Plus: losing to China on capability is recoverable; losing control of frontier systems isn't. Also, chips/energy advantage. Keep it to <=120 words.

For Q&A #4 (CAISI funding): $100M/yr is a real increase over ~$10M FY2026. But funding a standards shop doesn't stop the race. Our support is conditional: CAISI as the enforcement body for the moratorium - licensing, certification testing, verifying the wind-down, with fee authority. If the sponsors keep CAISI advisory-only, no funding level makes it adequate. Also note the House Science version authorizes $20M/yr - hmm, do I need that? It could be a useful factual note ("the Science Committee's version of the CAISI bill, advanced in June, authorizes $20M/yr through 2032") - shows the number is unsettled. Maybe include briefly. It's verified via Roll Call.

Now, the letter structure (1,500-2,200 words):
- Letterhead block: Frontier Restraint Coalition, date (say, 26 Oct 2026? The letter goes out "the following week" after Fri 23 Oct sign-off - so week of 26 Oct. I'll date it 26 October 2026 or leave a [date] placeholder. Hmm. As a draft for ED sign-off, I could put "[DATE - ED to confirm; targeting Mon 26 Oct]" - cleaner to use a placeholder note. Actually, work order says "due to Executive Director Fri 23 Oct for sign-off; letter goes to GAAIA@mail.house.gov the following week." I'll date it Monday 26 October 2026 with a bracketed note to confirm the send date. Let me use "October 26, 2026" with a footnote-style editorial note in the draft? Editor notes in brackets are normal for drafts. I'll include a small "[Draft note: ...]" at the top instead of inside the letter body.

- Addressees: Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA-23) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA-03). Sent via GAAIA@mail.house.gov.
- Re: FRC comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released June 4, 2026)
- Body:
  1. Who we are (coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals, independent researchers; 501(c)(4)). Voice from the OSTP comment: "parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers." 
  2. Bottom line up front: oppose as drafted; the bill's premise - that transparency and reporting can manage frontier risk - is the flaw; ask to replace frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a moratorium. Use messaging guide language: "existential threat", "pause", "wind down", "no safe path on the current trajectory."
  3. What the draft gets right (be fair): whistleblower protections (Sec. 113), codifying CAISI (Sec. 102), incident reporting concept, IVO third-party audit concept, weight-security GAO review, NAIRR, testbeds - we don't oppose all of it; supports as building blocks. # Stop the race, then write the rules
## FRC position on the Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft - October 2026

What's happening: Obernolte-Trahan draft (June 4) - first bipartisan federal framework for frontier AI; frontier provisions also introduced as FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925); E&C action possible this fall.

The problem: The draft's core is transparency and reporting (Secs. 111-112). Nothing in it stops a training run. 3. Personal accountability. Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
4. Strike Sec. 121 preemption. Let California, New York and Illinois keep their laws.
5. Keep the good parts. Whistleblower protections (Sec. 113), AI-fraud penalties (Secs. 131-132), research capacity (Title IV) - and make CAISI (Sec. 102) the moratorium's enforcement body, not a voluntary standards shop.

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for taking comment before introduction. Frontier AI is the hardest policy problem this Congress faces, and the draft treats it seriously. We are writing to be equally serious about where it falls short.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers working for binding limits on frontier AI. In March 2025 we filed comments on the Office of Science and Technology Policy's AI Action Plan request for information, asking then for binding pre-deployment testing and for the states' right to act. We write in the same spirit, and with the same plain language our members use.

Our bottom line: we oppose the bill as drafted. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium - an immediate pause on training the most powerful systems until Congress certifies they can be reliably controlled, and a wind-down of the most powerful systems already released.

**Where we agree with the draft**

The draft concedes the central point of this debate: that a line exists above which ordinary rules do not suffice. Section 101 draws that line at 10^26 computing operations - the draft's own definition of a "frontier model." We agree with the line. The dispute is what follows from it. The draft asks developers above the line to describe what they are doing. We ask them to stop, prove control, and only then proceed.

Several parts of the draft deserve to survive in any final bill. Section 113's whistleblower protections are strong, and we support them. Sections 131 and 132 raise penalties for AI-enabled fraud and for impersonating government officials; we support those too. Title IV's testbeds and NAIRR codification build research capacity the country needs, and the GAO review of model-weight security in Section 122 addresses a real and neglected danger. None of that is at issue in our opposition.

**Why the core of the draft cannot carry the weight**

The heart of the draft is Section 111 (transparency) and Section 112 (independent verification organization audits). We have read them as a coalition of parents and researchers, and we ask the sponsors to walk through what they actually require:

Section 111 tells large frontier developers to write their own safety plans, publish them, and report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI Director within 15 days - 24 hours to law enforcement only where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 112 tells them to hire licensed outside auditors twice a year to check whether they are following their own plans.

Every one of those duties lands after the fact. Reports describe incidents that have already happened. Audits check compliance with a plan the developer wrote itself. The draft's own definition of "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" (Section 101) is a balancing test - anticipated benefits outweighing catastrophic risks - which is a judgment call, not a demonstration of control. And nothing in either section slows, pauses, or stops a single training run. A developer could comply with Sections 111 and 112 completely and still build and release a system that no one - including its maker - can control.

That is the whole of our objection. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory, and this draft leaves the trajectory untouched.

The enforcement design confirms it. Violations of Section 111 carry civil penalties up to $1 million per violation, with each day a separate violation (Section 111(i)) - a cost of doing business for companies spending billions on training runs. There is no criminal liability anywhere in the frontier provisions, for anyone. CAISI, codified in Section 102 with $100 million a year, is directed to write voluntary guidelines and run evaluations. Advice is not enforcement. We support CAISI in one role only: as the enforcement body for a moratorium.

**On Section 121, we ask you to strike it**

Section 121 would block any state law that specifically regulates the development of AI models for three years. Per your offices' own description, that would federalize frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois, and reach laws like California's AB 2013 (training-data disclosure) and parts of SB 942.

We oppose Section 121 outright, for three reasons.

First, the floor is weaker than what it replaces. New York's RAISE Act requires critical incidents to be reported within 72 hours. The draft's federal standard is 15 days. Preempting state law to impose slower reporting is not a national standard; it is a step backward.

Second, the freeze lands mid-stride. California's SB 53 has been in effect since January. New York's RAISE Act takes effect in January 2027. Illinois's SB 315 was signed in July. Section 121 would freeze all three for three years - and if Congress fails to reauthorize the transparency provisions at the end of that window (they sunset too), the country will be left with neither the state laws nor the federal ones.

Third, voters have already weighed in. In our August 2026 national survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Congress has been here before: last year the Senate stripped a ten-year state-law moratorium from the reconciliation bill by a vote of 99 to 1. Preemption is the part of this debate Congress has already rejected once. Please do not revive it here.

**What we ask you to build instead**

We ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a moratorium with four parts:

1. Pause. An immediate halt on training any model above 10^26 computing operations - the draft's own line - until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Certification means a developer can show control before it builds, not describe its risks after.

2. Wind down. Frontier models already deployed that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released - Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen - whose weights, once downloaded, cannot be recalled. U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them. The largest open-weight releases of 2026 came from Chinese labs; a pause that stops at our border would not protect Americans, and ours does not.

3. Personal criminal liability. Executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause face criminal penalties. Sixty-six percent of voters support criminal penalties when these systems cause mass harm. Civil fines alone will not stop a race this profitable.

4. CAISI as the enforcement body. Licensing independent testers, running certification, verifying the wind-down, and referring violations for prosecution. We support CAISI's funding - indeed its current appropriation is about $10 million a year, so $100 million is a real upgrade - but only in that role.

**A word on timing**

We understand the frontier-governance provisions have also been introduced as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, now before the Energy and Commerce Committee. Everything above applies to that bill with equal force, and we would welcome the chance to discuss it as the Committee's schedule allows.

**Closing**

Some will read this letter as asking Congress to do something radical. It is not radical. In June, Anthropic - a company building frontier systems - said publicly that "it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause" frontier development, because systems that can build their own successors may put human control at risk. When the developers themselves ask for the option to stop, the only question is whether the pause comes by design or by disaster. In our August survey, 74 percent of voters said companies should have to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, and 49 percent said they support a temporary halt outright. The public is not the obstacle. The draft is not yet equal to the public.

We would welcome the chance to meet with your staff, to share the full survey toplines and crosstabs, and to connect you with our members - parents, nurses, machinists, pastors and researchers - who live with the stakes of this decision. Thank you for the bipartisan effort this draft represents. We would rather argue with you about how to stop the race than about whether to.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

Full letter text:

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft)

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for taking comment before introduction. Frontier AI is the hardest policy problem this Congress faces, and the draft treats it seriously. We are writing to be equally serious about where it falls short.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers working for binding limits on frontier AI. In March 2025 we filed comments on the Office of Science and Technology Policy's AI Action Plan request for information, asking then for binding pre-deployment testing and for the states' right to act. We write in the same spirit, and with the same plain language our members use.

Our bottom line: we oppose the bill as drafted. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium - an immediate pause on training the most powerful systems until Congress certifies they can be reliably controlled, and a wind-down of the most powerful systems already released.

**Where we agree with the draft**

The draft concedes the central point of this debate: that a line exists above which ordinary rules do not suffice. Section 101 draws that line at 10^26 computing operations - the draft's own definition of a "frontier model." We agree with the line. The dispute is what follows from it. The draft asks developers above the line to describe what they are doing. We ask them to stop, prove control, and only then proceed.

Several parts of the draft deserve to survive in any final bill. Section 113's whistleblower protections are strong, and we support them. Sections 131 and 132 raise penalties for AI-enabled fraud and for impersonating government officials; we support those too. Title IV's testbeds and NAIRR codification build research capacity the country needs, and the GAO review of model-weight security in Section 122 addresses a real and neglected danger. None of that is at issue in our opposition.

**Why the core of the draft cannot carry the weight**

The heart of the draft is Section 111 (transparency) and Section 112 (independent verification organization audits). We have read them as a coalition of parents and researchers, and we ask the sponsors to walk through what they actually require:

Section 111 tells large frontier developers to write their own safety plans, publish them, and report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI Director within 15 days - 24 hours to law enforcement only where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 112 tells them to hire licensed outside auditors twice a year to check whether they are following their own plans.

Every one of those duties lands after the fact. Reports describe incidents that have already happened. Audits check compliance with a plan the developer wrote itself. The draft's own definition of "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" (Section 101) is a balancing test - anticipated benefits outweighing catastrophic risks - which is a judgment call, not a demonstration of control. And nothing in either section slows, pauses, or stops a single training run. A developer could comply with Sections 111 and 112 completely and still build and release a system that no one - including its maker - can control.

That is the whole of our objection. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory, and this draft leaves the trajectory untouched.

The enforcement design confirms it. Violations of Section 111 carry civil penalties up to $1 million per violation, with each day a separate violation (Section 111(i)) - a cost of doing business for companies spending billions on training runs. There is no criminal liability anywhere in the frontier provisions, for anyone. CAISI, codified in Section 102 with $100 million a year, is directed to write voluntary guidelines and run evaluations. Advice is not enforcement. We support CAISI in one role only: as the enforcement body for a moratorium.

**On Section 121, we ask you to strike it**

Section 121 would block any state law that specifically regulates the development of AI models for three years. Per your offices' own description, that would federalize frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois, and reach laws like California's AB 2013 (training-data disclosure) and parts of SB 942.

We oppose Section 121 outright, for three reasons.

First, the floor is weaker than what it replaces. New York's RAISE Act requires critical incidents to be reported within 72 hours. The draft's federal standard is 15 days. Preempting state law to impose slower reporting is not a national standard; it is a step backward.

Second, the freeze lands mid-stride. California's SB 53 has been in effect since January. New York's RAISE Act takes effect in January 2027. Illinois's SB 315 was signed in July. Section 121 would freeze all three for three years - and if Congress fails to reauthorize the transparency provisions at the end of that window (they sunset too), the country will be left with neither the state laws nor the federal ones.

Third, voters have already weighed in. In our August 2026 national survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Congress has been here before: last year the Senate stripped a ten-year state-law moratorium from the reconciliation bill by a vote of 99 to 1. Preemption is the part of this debate Congress has already rejected once. Please do not revive it here.

**What we ask you to build instead**

We ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a moratorium with four parts:

1. Pause. An immediate halt on training any model above 10^26 computing operations - the draft's own line - until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Certification means a developer can show control before it builds, not describe its risks after.

2. Wind down. Frontier models already deployed that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released - Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen - whose weights, once downloaded, cannot be recalled. U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them. The largest open-weight releases of 2026 came from Chinese labs; a pause that stops at our border would not protect Americans, and ours does not.

3. Personal criminal liability. Executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause face criminal penalties. Sixty-six percent of voters support criminal penalties when these systems cause mass harm. Civil fines alone will not stop a race this profitable.

4. CAISI as the enforcement body. Licensing independent testers, running certification, verifying the wind-down, and referring violations for prosecution. We support CAISI's funding - indeed its current appropriation is about $10 million a year, so $100 million is a real upgrade - but only in that role.

**A word on timing**

We understand the frontier-governance provisions have also been introduced as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, now before the Energy and Commerce Committee. Everything above applies to that bill with equal force, and we would welcome the chance to discuss it as the Committee's schedule allows.

**Closing**

Some will read this letter as asking Congress to do something radical. It is not radical. In June, Anthropic - a company building frontier systems - said publicly that "it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause" frontier development, because systems that can build their own successors may put human control at risk. When the developers themselves ask for the option to stop, the only question is whether the pause comes by design or by disaster. In our August survey, 74 percent of voters said companies should have to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, and 49 percent said they support a temporary halt outright. The public is not the obstacle. The draft is not yet equal to the public.

We would welcome the chance to meet with your staff, to share the full survey toplines and crosstabs, and to connect you with our members - parents, nurses, machinists, pastors and researchers - who live with the stakes of this decision. Thank you for the bipartisan effort this draft represents. We would rather argue with you about how to stop the race than about whether to.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

**Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft)**

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for taking comment before introduction. Frontier AI is the hardest policy problem this Congress faces, and your draft treats it seriously. We are writing to be equally serious about where it falls short.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers working for binding limits on frontier AI. In March 2025 we filed comments on the Office of Science and Technology Policy's AI Action Plan request for information, asking then for binding pre-deployment testing of frontier systems, protection for the states' right to act, and whistleblower protections. We write in the same spirit, in the same plain language our members use.

Our bottom line: we oppose the bill as drafted. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium — an immediate pause on training the most powerful systems until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled, together with a wind-down of the most powerful systems already in the world.

## Where we agree with the draft

The draft concedes the central point of this debate: that a line exists above which ordinary rules do not suffice. Section 101 draws that line at 10^26 computing operations — the draft's own definition of a "frontier model" — and builds a special set of duties around it. We agree with the line. The disagreement is about what follows from it. The draft asks developers above the line to describe what they are doing. We ask them to stop, prove control, and only then proceed.

Several parts of the draft deserve to survive into any final bill, and we say so plainly. Section 113's whistleblower protections are strong, non-waivable and long overdue; we support them. Sections 131 and 132 raise penalties for AI-enabled fraud and for impersonating government officials; we support those. Title IV's testbeds and NAIRR codification build research capacity the country needs, and the Section 321 review of model-weight and open-source security addresses a real and neglected danger. None of that is at issue in our opposition.

## Why the core of the draft cannot carry the weight

The heart of the draft is Section 111 (transparency) and Section 112 (independent verification organization audits). Walk through what these sections actually require.

Section 111 tells large frontier developers to write, implement and publish their own "frontier AI framework" — their own plan for assessing catastrophic risk — within a year. All frontier developers must publish transparency reports, and the required contents are telling: the model's release date, the languages it supports, its output types, its intended use, and how to contact the developer. Critical safety incidents — stolen model weights, failed risk controls, loss of control of a model — are reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days, or within 24 hours to law enforcement only where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 112 then requires a licensed outside auditor, at least twice a year, to check whether the developer is following its own plan.

Every one of those duties lands after the fact. Reports describe incidents that have already happened. Audits check compliance with a plan the developer wrote itself. The draft's own definition of "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" (Section 101) is a balancing test — anticipated benefits outweighing catastrophic risks — which is a judgment call, not a demonstration of control. And nothing in either section slows, pauses or stops a single training run. A developer could comply with Sections 111 and 112 completely and still build and release a system that no one, including its maker, can control.

That is the whole of our objection. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory, and this draft leaves the trajectory untouched.

The draft's enforcement design confirms this. Violations of Section 111 carry civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day counted separately (Section 111(i)) — a cost of doing business for companies spending billions of dollars on training runs. There is no criminal liability anywhere in the frontier provisions, for anyone. CAISI, codified in Section 102 at $100 million a year, is directed to write voluntary guidelines, run evaluations and license auditors. Advice is not enforcement. We support CAISI in one role only: as the enforcement body for a moratorium.

Nor is the draft an outlier; it is the latest in a series of voluntary arrangements. The Administration's June executive order rests on reviews that developers may simply skip, with a thirty-day government look at new systems before release. The through-line of federal AI policy is "ask nicely." A bill that finally puts duties in statute should not stop at duties to describe.

## On Section 121, we ask you to strike it

Section 121 would block, for three years, any state law that specifically regulates the development of AI models. According to Rep. Trahan's office, it would federalize the frontier safety laws of California, New York and Illinois, and reach California's AB 2013 (training-data disclosure) and parts of SB 942 (AI transparency).

We oppose Section 121 outright, for three reasons.

First, the federal floor is weaker than what it replaces. Both regimes have a 24-hour clock for imminent dangers, but on the baseline New York's RAISE Act gives regulators 72 hours to hear about a critical safety incident, while the draft gives them 15 days. Preempting state law in order to impose slower reporting is not a national standard; it is a step backward.

Second, the freeze lands mid-stride. California's SB 53 has been in effect since January. New York's RAISE Act takes effect in January 2027. Illinois's SB 315 was signed in July. Section 121 would freeze all three for three years — and the federal obligations it substitutes sunset at the same three-year mark unless Congress reauthorizes them. If Congress fails to act on time, the country is left with neither the state laws nor the federal ones.

Third, the public has already weighed in. In our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters (fielded August 10–17; margin of error ±2.5 points), 63 percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Congress has been here before: last year the Senate stripped a ten-year state-law moratorium from the reconciliation bill by a vote of 99 to 1. Preemption is the part of this debate Congress has already rejected once. Please do not revive it here.

## What we ask you to build instead

Replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a moratorium built on four parts.

**1. Pause.** An immediate halt on training any model above 10^26 computing operations — the draft's own line — until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Certification means a developer can show control before it builds, not describe its risks after.

**2. Wind down.** Frontier models already deployed that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — whose weights, once downloaded, cannot be recalled. U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them. The largest open-weight releases of 2026 came from Chinese labs; a pause that stops at our border would not protect Americans, and ours does not.

**3. Personal criminal liability.** Executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause face criminal penalties. In our August survey, 66 percent of voters said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. Civil fines alone will not slow a race this profitable.

**4. CAISI as the enforcement body.** CAISI should license independent testers, run certification, verify the wind-down, and refer violations for prosecution. We do not oppose its funding — its current appropriation is roughly $10 million a year, so the draft's $100 million is a real upgrade — but we support it only in that role.

## The FRONTIER Act

We understand the frontier-governance provisions of this draft have now been introduced separately as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, before the Energy and Commerce Committee. Everything in this letter applies to that bill with equal force. We would welcome the chance to work with the Committee as it takes up that legislation.

## Closing

Some will read this letter as asking Congress to do something radical. It is not. In June, Anthropic — a company building frontier systems — said publicly that "it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause" frontier development, because systems that can build their own successors may put human control at risk. When developers themselves ask for the option to stop, the only question is whether the pause comes by design or after a disaster. In our August survey, 74 percent of voters said companies should have to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, 52 percent are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival, and 49 percent support a temporary halt outright. The public is not the obstacle. The draft, as written, is not yet equal to the public.

We would welcome the chance to meet with your staff, to share our full survey toplines and crosstabs, and to connect you with our members — parents, nurses, machinists, pastors and researchers — who live with the stakes of this decision every day. Thank you for the genuinely bipartisan effort this draft represents. We would rather argue with you about how to stop the race than about whether to.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

## Stop the race, then set the rules: replace GAAIA's reporting regime with a frontier pause

**What's happening.** Reps. Obernolte (R-CA) and Trahan (D-MA) released a 269-page discussion draft on June 4 to create the first federal framework for frontier AI. The sponsors are taking stakeholder comment at GAAIA@mail.house.gov, and the frontier-governance provisions are now also before E&C as the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925). Committee action is possible this fall.

**The problem.** The draft's core is transparency and reporting. Nothing in the bill slows a single training run. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. 1. **Pause, don't just report.** Replace the frontier-developer provisions (Secs. 111–112) with an immediate pause on training above 10^26 computing operations — the draft's own "frontier model" line — until Congress certifies these systems can be reliably controlled.
2. **Wind down what's already out.** Deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months — including open-weight releases (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen), whose weights cannot be recalled once downloaded. U.S. cloud providers stop serving them.
3. **Personal accountability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause.
4. **Strike Sec. 121 preemption.** Let California, New York and Illinois keep the laws they have already enacted.
5. **Keep the good parts.** Whistleblower protections (Sec. 113), AI-fraud penalties (Secs. 131–132), research capacity (Title IV) — and repurpose CAISI (Sec. 102) as the moratorium's enforcement body, not a voluntary standards shop.

**Bottom line.** There is no safe path on the current trajectory. A reporting regime that leaves the race intact leaves the threat intact.

**Contact:** Frontier Restraint Coalition policy team — [contact to be added by comms before distribution].

{"content": "# Staff Q&A — anticipated questions on FRC's GAAIA position

*Prep for Hill meetings, keyed to the four questions in the 2 Oct briefing. Answers ≤120 words each. Positions per messaging guide v4; facts checked 16 Oct 2026. Draft for Executive Director sign-off — speaker notes, not for distribution.*

---

**1. "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"** *(Majority E&C staff)*

Because every duty in the draft lands after the fact. Reporting describes incidents that have already happened. Audits check whether a company followed a plan it wrote itself. The draft's own definition of "acceptable" risk mitigation is a benefits-versus-risks judgment call, not proof of control. And nothing in the bill slows a single training run. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat: no developer can show its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does. Even Anthropic said in June the world needs the option to pause. CAISI as drafted writes voluntary guidelines — we support it only as the moratorium's enforcement arm.

---

**2. "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"** *(Minority staff, Trahan-aligned)*

Dropping preemption would fix one serious flaw, and we'd give a revised text a fresh look. But our opposition doesn't rest on preemption alone: transparency and reporting are not restraint, and without a pause the race — and the threat — stays fully intact. On preemption itself, we oppose it at any length. Three years would freeze California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois's SB 315 mid-phase-in, for a federal floor that is weaker in places: 15-day incident reporting instead of New York's 72 hours. Sixty-three percent of voters say federal law should not block state AI safety laws. The sponsors narrowed preemption in H.R. 9925; we still oppose it there.

---

**3. "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"** *(Senate Commerce staff)*

The race already includes China — the open-weight frontier is now largely set there. The largest open releases of 2026 came from Chinese labs: Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4, GLM-5.2, Qwen 3.8. That is exactly why our moratorium doesn't stop at the border: uncertified open-weight models would be wound down in the U.S., and American cloud providers would stop serving them. The competitiveness argument also assumes the race can be run safely. No developer — American or Chinese — can show that. Losing a capability race is recoverable; losing control of frontier systems may not be. The country that certifies control before it builds sets the standard everyone else has to meet.

---

**4. "CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"** *(Appropriations staff)*

$100 million a year for FY2027–29 is a real increase over the roughly $10 million CAISI received in FY2026, and the fee authority is sensible. But the level matters less than the authorities. As drafted, CAISI writes voluntary guidelines, runs evaluations and licenses auditors; it cannot stop anything, and developers can decline its advice. We support CAISI in one role: the enforcement body for a frontier moratorium — licensing independent testers, running certification, verifying the wind-down, and referring violations for prosecution. If the sponsors keep it advisory, no funding level makes it adequate. Worth noting: the House Science version advanced in June authorizes only $20 million a year, so the number is still unsettled.

---

*Sources for facts used above: draft sections 101, 102, 111, 112, 121 (sponsors' section-by-section); NY RAISE Act 72-hour reporting (as amended Mar 2026); IL SB 315 signed 6 Jul 2026; Anthropic statement 4 Jun 2026 (Reuters/AP); CAISI FY2026 appropriation (CJS appropriations; Roll Call 26 Jun 2026); FRC Aug 2026 survey (n=1,512, MOE ±2.5); open-weight releases (Kimi K3 27 Jul 2026; DeepSeek V4; GLM-5.2 Jun 2026; Qwen 3.8 Aug 2026).*

# Comment letter — Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

> **Draft notes for the Executive Director (not part of the letter).**
> Prepared 16 Oct 2026 for sign-off Fri 23 Oct; to go to **GAAIA@mail.house.gov** the week of 26 Oct. Send date assumed Mon 26 Oct — please confirm.
> Section numbers verified against the sponsors' section-by-section summary (obernolte.house.gov / trahan.house.gov) and the discussion-draft table of contents; this resolves the "TODO" flagged in the 2 Oct staff summary.
> The short section headed "The FRONTIER Act" references H.R. 9925 (introduced 23 Jul 2026), which now carries the draft's frontier-governance provisions. Daniel was out of queue on whether to include it; it is in per drafting judgment so the letter does not read as unaware of the introduced bill. Strike that section if you prefer the letter confined strictly to the discussion draft.
> External facts checked and sourced as of 16 Oct 2026: draft provisions and section numbers (sponsors' section-by-section; ArentFox Schiff analysis 16 Jun 2026; FedScoop 4 Jun 2026); CA SB 53 (signed 29 Sep 2025, effective 1 Jan 2026; 15-day/24-hour reporting); NY RAISE Act (amended Mar 2026, effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour/24-hour reporting); IL SB 315 (signed 6 Jul 2026); Anthropic pause statement (4 Jun 2026, Reuters/AP/Bloomberg); EO 14409 (2 Jun 2026); CAISI FY2026 appropriation (~$10M); Senate 99–1 vote stripping the 10-year state-law moratorium (Jul 2025). Polling: FRC Aug 2026 survey, n=1,512 registered voters, fielded 10–17 Aug, MOE ±2.5.

---

Frontier Restraint Coalition
Washington, DC

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft)**

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for taking comment before introduction. Frontier AI is the hardest policy problem this Congress faces, and your draft treats it seriously. We are writing to be equally serious about where it falls short.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers working for binding limits on frontier AI. In March 2025 we filed comments on the Office of Science and Technology Policy's AI Action Plan request for information, asking then for binding pre-deployment testing of frontier systems, protection for the states' right to act, and whistleblower protections. We write in the same spirit, in the same plain language our members use.

Our bottom line: we oppose the bill as drafted. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium — an immediate pause on training the most powerful systems until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled, together with a wind-down of the most powerful systems already in the world.

## Where we agree with the draft

The draft concedes the central point of this debate: that a line exists above which ordinary rules do not suffice. Section 101 draws that line at 10^26 computing operations — the draft's own definition of a "frontier model" — and builds a special set of duties around it. We agree with the line. The disagreement is about what follows from it. The draft asks developers above the line to describe what they are doing. We ask them to stop, prove control, and only then proceed.

Several parts of the draft deserve to survive into any final bill, and we say so plainly. Section 113's whistleblower protections are strong, non-waivable and long overdue; we support them. Sections 131 and 132 raise penalties for AI-enabled fraud and for impersonating government officials; we support those. Title IV's testbeds and NAIRR codification build research capacity the country needs, and the Section 321 review of model-weight and open-source security addresses a real and neglected danger. None of that is at issue in our opposition.

## Why the core of the draft cannot carry the weight

The heart of the draft is Section 111 (transparency) and Section 112 (independent verification organization audits). Walk through what these sections actually require.

Section 111 tells large frontier developers to write, implement and publish their own "frontier AI framework" — their own plan for assessing catastrophic risk — within a year. All frontier developers must publish transparency reports, and the required contents are telling: the model's release date, the languages it supports, its output types, its intended use, and how to contact the developer. Critical safety incidents — stolen model weights, failed risk controls, loss of control of a model — are reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days, or within 24 hours to law enforcement only where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 112 then requires a licensed outside auditor, at least twice a year, to check whether the developer is following its own plan.

Every one of those duties lands after the fact. Reports describe incidents that have already happened. Audits check compliance with a plan the developer wrote itself. The draft's own definition of "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" (Section 101) is a balancing test — anticipated benefits outweighing catastrophic risks — which is a judgment call, not a demonstration of control. And nothing in either section slows, pauses or stops a single training run. A developer could comply with Sections 111 and 112 completely and still build and release a system that no one, including its maker, can control.

That is the whole of our objection. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllabl
... [235 chars truncated] ...
enforcement design confirms this. Violations of Section 111 carry civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day counted separately (Section 111(i)) — a cost of doing business for developers whose frontier training runs already cost hundreds of millions of dollars, and are on their way past a billion. There is no criminal liability anywhere in the frontier provisions, for anyone. CAISI, codified in Section 102 at $100 million a year, is directed to write voluntary guidelines, run evaluations and license auditors. Advice is not enforcement. We support CAISI in one role only: as the enforcement body for a moratorium.

Nor is the draft an outlier; it is the latest in a series of voluntary arrangements. The Administration's June executive order rests on reviews that developers may simply skip, with a thirty-day government look at new systems before release. The through-line of federal AI policy is "ask nicely." A bill that finally puts duties in statute should not stop at duties to describe.

## On Section 121, we ask you to strike it

Section 121 would block, for three years, any state law that specifically regulates the development of AI models. According to Rep. Trahan's office, it would federalize the frontier safety laws of California, New York and Illinois, and reach California's AB 2013 (training-data disclosure) and parts of SB 942 (AI transparency).

We oppose Section 121 outright, for three reasons.

First, the federal floor is weaker than what it replaces. Both regimes have a 24-hour clock for imminent dangers, but on the baseline New York's RAISE Act gives regulators 72 hours to hear about a critical safety incident, while the draft gives them 15 days. Preempting state law in order to impose slower reporting is not a national standard; it is a step backward.

Second, the freeze lands mid-stride. California's SB 53 has been in effect since January. New York's RAISE Act takes effect in January 2027. Illinois's SB 315 was signed in July. Section 121 would freeze all three for three years — and the federal obligations it substitutes sunset at the same three-year mark unless Congress reauthorizes them. If Congress fails to act on time, the country is left with neither the state laws nor the federal ones.

Third, the public has already weighed in. In our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters (fielded August 10–17; margin of error ±2.5 points), 63 percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Congress has been here before: last year the Senate stripped a ten-year state-law moratorium from the reconciliation bill by a vote of 99 to 1. Preemption is the part of this debate Congress has already rejected once. Please do not revive it here.

## What we ask you to build instead

Replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a moratorium built on four parts.

**1. Pause.** An immediate halt on training any model above 10^26 computing operations — the draft's own line — until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Certification means a developer can show control before it builds, not describe its risks after.

**2. Wind down.** Frontier models already deployed that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — whose weights, once downloaded, cannot be recalled. U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them. The largest open-weight releases of 2026 came from Chinese labs; a pause that stops at our border would not protect Americans, and ours does not.

**3. Personal criminal liability.** Executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause face criminal penalties. In our August survey, 66 percent of voters said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. Civil fines alone will not slow a race this profitable.

**4. CAISI as the enforcement body.** CAISI should license independent testers, run certification, verify the wind-down, and refer violations for prosecution. We do not oppose its funding — its current appropriation is roughly $10 million a year, so the draft's $100 million is a real upgrade — but we support it only in that role.

## The FRONTIER Act

We understand the frontier-governance provisions of this draft have now been introduced separately as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, before the Energy and Commerce Committee. Everything in this letter applies to that bill with equal force. We would welcome the chance to work with the Committee as it takes up that legislation.

## Closing

Some will read this letter as asking Congress to do something radical. It is not. In June, Anthropic — a company building frontier systems — said publicly that "it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause" frontier development, because systems that can build their own successors may put human control at risk. When developers themselves ask for the option to stop, the only question is whether the pause comes by design or after a disaster. In our August survey, 74 percent said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, 52 percent are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival, and 49 percent support a temporary halt outright. The public is not the obstacle. The draft, as written, is not yet equal to the public.

We would welcome the chance to meet with your staff, to share our full survey toplines and crosstabs, and to connect you with our members — parents, nurses, machinists, pastors and researchers — who live with the stakes of this decision every day. Thank you for the genuinely bipartisan effort this draft represents. We would rather argue with you about how to stop the race than about whether to.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
