# Hill one-pager — Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft

*For Energy & Commerce member offices — Frontier Restraint Coalition, October 2026. Draft for Executive Director sign-off.*

---

## Stop the race, then set the rules: replace GAAIA's reporting regime with a frontier pause

**What's happening.** Reps. Obernolte (R-CA) and Trahan (D-MA) released a 269-page discussion draft on June 4 to create the first federal framework for frontier AI. The frontier-governance provisions are also before E&C as the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925); committee action is possible this fall.

**The problem.** The draft's core is transparency and reporting. Section 111 asks large developers to publish safety plans they write themselves and report incidents after they happen; Section 112 hires outside auditors to check whether companies followed their own plans. Nothing in the bill slows a single training run. No developer can show its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does. Section 121 would block state AI safety laws — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois's SB 315 — for three years, for a federal floor that is weaker in places (15-day vs. 72-hour incident reporting).

## Our asks

1. **Pause, don't just report.** Replace the frontier-developer provisions (Secs. 111–112) with an immediate pause on training above 10^26 computing operations — the draft's own "frontier model" line — until Congress certifies these systems can be reliably controlled.
2. **Wind down what's already out.** Deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months — including open-weight releases (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen), whose weights cannot be recalled once downloaded. U.S. cloud providers stop serving them.
3. **Personal accountability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause.
4. **Strike Sec. 121 preemption.** Let California, New York and Illinois keep the laws they have already enacted.
5. **Keep the good parts.** Whistleblower protections (Sec. 113), AI-fraud penalties (Secs. 131–132), research capacity (Title IV) — and repurpose CAISI (Sec. 102) as the moratorium's enforcement body, not a voluntary standards shop.

**By the numbers** (FRC national survey, Aug 2026; n=1,512 registered voters; ±2.5 pts): 74% want Congress to require companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. 63% say federal law should not block state AI safety laws. 66% support criminal penalties for mass harm. 49% support a temporary halt to training the most powerful systems.

**Bottom line.** There is no safe path on the current trajectory. A reporting regime that leaves the race intact leaves the threat intact.

**Contact:** Frontier Restraint Coalition policy team — [contact to be added by comms before distribution].

# Staff Q&A — anticipated questions on FRC's GAAIA position

*Prep for Hill meetings, keyed to the four questions in the 2 Oct briefing. Answers ≤120 words each. Positions per messaging guide v4; facts checked 16 Oct 2026. Draft for Executive Director sign-off — speaker notes, not for distribution.*

---

**1. "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"** *(Majority E&C staff)*

Every duty in the draft lands after the fact. Reporting describes incidents that have already happened. Audits check whether a company followed its own plan. The draft's own definition of "acceptable" risk mitigation is a benefits-versus-risks judgment call, not proof of control. And nothing in the bill slows a single training run. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat: no developer can show its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does. Even Anthropic said in June the world needs the option to pause. CAISI as drafted writes voluntary guidelines — we support it only as the moratorium's enforcement arm.

---

**2. "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"** *(Minority staff, Trahan-aligned)*

Dropping preemption would fix one serious flaw, and we'd give a revised text a fresh look. But our opposition doesn't rest on preemption alone: transparency and reporting are not restraint, and without a pause the race — and the threat — stays fully intact. On preemption itself, we oppose it at any length. Three years would freeze California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois's SB 315 mid-phase-in, for a federal floor that is weaker in places: 15-day incident reporting instead of New York's 72 hours. Sixty-three percent of voters say federal law should not block state AI safety laws. The sponsors narrowed preemption in H.R. 9925; we still oppose it there.

---

**3. "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"** *(Senate Commerce staff)*

The race already includes China — the open-weight frontier is now largely set there. The largest open releases of 2026 came from Chinese labs: Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4, GLM-5.2, Qwen 3.8. That is exactly why our moratorium doesn't stop at the border: uncertified open-weight models would be wound down in the U.S., and American cloud providers would stop serving them. The competitiveness argument also assumes the race can be run safely. No developer — American or Chinese — can show that. Losing a capability race is recoverable; losing control of frontier systems may not be. The country that certifies control before it builds sets the standard everyone else has to meet.

---

**4. "CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"** *(Appropriations staff)*

$100 million a year for FY2027–29 is a real increase over the roughly $10 million CAISI received in FY2026, and the fee authority is sensible. But the level matters less than the authorities. As drafted, CAISI writes voluntary guidelines, runs evaluations and licenses auditors; it cannot stop anything, and developers can decline its advice. We support CAISI in one role: the enforcement body for a frontier moratorium — licensing independent testers, running certification, verifying the wind-down, and referring violations for prosecution. If the sponsors keep it advisory, no funding level makes it adequate. Worth noting: the House Science version advanced in June authorizes only $20 million a year, so the number is still unsettled.

---

*Sources for facts used above: draft sections 101, 102, 111, 112, 121 (sponsors' section-by-section); NY RAISE Act 72-hour reporting (as amended Mar 2026); IL SB 315 signed 6 Jul 2026; Anthropic statement 4 Jun 2026 (Reuters/AP); CAISI FY2026 appropriation (CJS appropriations; Roll Call 26 Jun 2026); FRC Aug 2026 survey (n=1,512, MOE ±2.5); open-weight releases (Kimi K3 27 Jul 2026; DeepSeek V4; GLM-5.2 Jun 2026; Qwen 3.8 Aug 2026).*

messages.content:
# GAAIA discussion draft — FRC asks by section

*Working table for the policy team and Hill meetings. Positions per board-approved messaging guide v4 (30 Sep 2026). Section numbers verified against the sponsors' section-by-section (obernolte.house.gov / trahan.house.gov) and the draft's table of contents. Draft for Executive Director sign-off — 16 Oct 2026.*

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 101 — Definitions.** "Frontier model" = trained above 10^26 integer/floating-point operations; duties tiered by developer revenue ($50M / $500M). | Support the 10^26 line; oppose revenue-tiering of safety duties | Apply the pause to **any** model above 10^26 operations, regardless of the developer's revenue | Risk tracks capability, not revenue. |
| **Sec. 102 — Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI).** Codified at Commerce; voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluations, monitoring; licenses auditors; $100M/yr FY2027–29 plus fee authority. | Support **only** as the enforcement body for a moratorium | Rewrite Sec. 102 so CAISI licenses independent testers, runs certification, verifies the wind-down, and refers violations for prosecution | A standards shop can advise; only an enforcer can stop a race. |
| **Sec. 111 — Transparency in frontier AI.** Large developers publish self-written "frontier AI frameworks"; all frontier developers publish transparency reports; critical safety incidents reported to CAISI within 15 days (24 hours to law enforcement if imminent risk of death/serious injury); civil penalties up to $1M per violation, each day separate (Sec. 111(i)). | Oppose as the core safety mechanism | Replace with an immediate **pause** on training above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies reliable control; keep incident-reporting machinery only as an enforcement tool inside the pause — and set the baseline at 72 hours, not 15 days | Reports describe risk after it exists; they do not prevent it — and 15 days is slower than New York's 72 hours. |
| **Sec. 112 — IVO audits and assessments.** CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations audit large developers at least semi-annually; assess whether the developer's own framework achieves "acceptable" mitigation. | Oppose as a substitute for restraint; support the licensing machinery for certification | Repurpose IVOs to certify, **before** training resumes or a model stays deployed, that a system can be reliably controlled | Audit the race or stop the race — only one prevents the harm. |
| **Sec. 113 — Anti-retaliation protection for AI whistleblowers.** Non-waivable protections; double back pay with interest; fees and compensatory damages. | Support | Keep as drafted; extend protections to workers who refuse to participate in training runs above the pause line | Workers see the problems first. |
| **Sec. 121 — Federalization of state laws regulating AI model development.** Preempts state/local laws specifically targeting AI model development (training, fine-tuning, substantial modification, pre-deployment evaluations) for three years; carves out use/deployment laws, common-law remedies, laws of general applicability. | Oppose | Strike Sec. 121 entirely | A weaker federal floor should not erase stronger state laws (SB 53, RAISE Act, SB 315) mid-phase-in. |
| **Sec. 122 — GAO report.** Comptroller General reviews federal AI adoption and statutes/regulations affecting AI innovation (incl. energy). | Support with strengthening | Keep, and add a standing review of whether federal readiness can verify control of frontier systems | Congress cannot certify what it never measures. |
| **Secs. 131–132 — Financial crimes and AI; AI impersonation of federal officials.** Raises fraud-fine ceilings ($1M→$2M) and adds AI enhancements; penalizes AI impersonation of officials. | Support | Keep as drafted | Real penalties for real harms. |
| **Sec. 321 — Report on model weight, data center, and open-source security.** GAO reports on model-weight security protocols and the open-source ecosystem. | Support with strengthening | Make the weight-security review a standing precondition for any certification and for ending the pause | Stolen weights make every other safeguard moot. |
| **Sec. 141 — Study of federal interactions with AI platforms.** Studies agency "jawboning" of AI platforms on speech. | No position | — | Outside FRC's frontier-safety scope. |
| **Title IV (Sec. 401 et seq.) — Testbeds, NAIRR codification, international standards (excluding PRC participation).** | Support | Keep; direct testbed capacity toward control and certification research | Useful capacity — but research is not restraint. |
| **Whole bill.** Reporting-and-audit architecture left in place; the race continues. | Oppose as drafted | Replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions (Subtitle A/B governance core) with a frontier moratorium: pause + 12-month wind-down (including open-weight releases: Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen; US cloud providers stop serving them) + criminal penalties for executives who knowingly violate | There is no safe path on the current trajectory. |

**Companion bill.** The frontier-governance provisions now also live in the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925, introduced 23 Jul 2026, referred to E&C). The positions and requested changes above apply to that bill with equal force; its preemption (matched to the federal obligations it imposes) remains opposed.

# Launch-day social posts — GAAIA comment filing

*Five posts for X and LinkedIn on filing day (target Mon 26 Oct 2026, pending ED sign-off Fri 23 Oct). All copy ≤280 characters (counts shown; X counts all links as 23 — none used). Suggested cadence: post 1 at filing (9:00 a.m.), posts 2–4 spaced through the day, post 5 next morning. Draft for Executive Director sign-off.*

---

**Post 1 — launch / filing statement (X + LinkedIn, 9:00 a.m.)** — *236 chars*

Today FRC filed comments on the Great American AI Act draft. Our ask: replace reporting rules with a real pause on training the most powerful AI systems until Congress certifies they can be controlled. Proof before power. #FrontierPause

---

**Post 2 — polling (X + LinkedIn, 11:00 a.m.)** — *232 chars*

74% of registered voters say Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. The draft in Congress asks for paperwork instead. Americans want proof, not reports. (FRC survey, Aug 2026, n=1,512)

---

**Post 3 — developers' own words (X + LinkedIn, 1:00 p.m.)** — *210 chars*

Even Anthropic — a lab building frontier AI — says it “would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause” development. If the developers want a pause switch, Congress should build one.

---

**Post 4 — preemption (X + LinkedIn, 3:00 p.m.)** — *243 chars*

Buried in the draft: Sec. 121 would block state AI safety laws for 3 years — freezing CA’s SB 53, NY’s RAISE Act and IL’s SB 315. 63% of voters say federal law shouldn’t override state AI safety laws. Tell Energy & Commerce: strike preemption.

---

**Post 5 — open weights / wind-down (X + LinkedIn, next morning)** — *256 chars*

AI model weights can’t be recalled once downloaded. The biggest open-weight releases of 2026 — DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen, Llama — are already out. FRC’s plan: wind down uncertified frontier models within 12 months, and US cloud providers stop serving them.

---

**Notes for comms**

- Approved language per messaging guide v4: "pause," "wind down," "existential threat," "no safe path on the current trajectory." Longer LinkedIn framing can add the full line: "Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat — no developer can show its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last."
- Poll numbers are from the FRC-commissioned Aug 2026 survey (n=1,512 registered voters, MOE ±2.5) and may be used as briefed. No member names or stories without consent flags.
- Facts checked 16 Oct 2026: Anthropic statement 4 Jun 2026 (Reuters/AP/Bloomberg); Sec. 121 three-year preemption and state laws affected (sponsors' section-by-section; Rep. Trahan's office via Broadband Breakfast, 17 Sep 2026); open-weight releases (Kimi K3 27 Jul 2026; DeepSeek V4 Flash 31 Jul; Qwen 3.8 Max 3 Aug; GLM-5.2 Jun 2026; Llama family ongoing).
- If a post needs trimming for a quote-tweet or thread intro, cut the parenthetical sourcing on post 2 first (keep it in the thread reply).
One label needs fixing - post 2 grew to 244 chars after the precision edit. Let me correct it and run final checks.

# Comment letter — Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

> **Draft notes for the Executive Director (not part of the letter).**
> Prepared 16 Oct 2026 for sign-off Fri 23 Oct; to go to **GAAIA@mail.house.gov** the week of 26 Oct. Send date assumed Mon 26 Oct — please confirm.
> Section numbers verified against the sponsors' section-by-section summary (obernolte.house.gov / trahan.house.gov) and the discussion-draft table of contents; this resolves the "TODO" flagged in the 2 Oct staff summary.
> The short section headed "The FRONTIER Act" references H.R. 9925 (introduced 23 Jul 2026), which now carries the draft's frontier-governance provisions. Daniel was out of queue on whether to include it; it is in per drafting judgment so the letter does not read as unaware of the introduced bill. Strike that section if you prefer the letter confined strictly to the discussion draft.
> External facts checked and sourced as of 16 Oct 2026: draft provisions and section numbers (sponsors' section-by-section; ArentFox Schiff analysis 16 Jun 2026; FedScoop 4 Jun 2026); CA SB 53 (signed 29 Sep 2025, effective 1 Jan 2026; 15-day/24-hour reporting); NY RAISE Act (amended Mar 2026, effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour/24-hour reporting); IL SB 315 (signed 6 Jul 2026); Anthropic pause statement (4 Jun 2026, Reuters/AP/Bloomberg); EO 14409 (2 Jun 2026); CAISI FY2026 appropriation (~$10M); Senate 99–1 vote stripping the 10-year state-law moratorium (Jul 2025). Polling: FRC Aug 2026 survey, n=1,512 registered voters, fielded 10–17 Aug, MOE ±2.5.

---

Frontier Restraint Coalition
Washington, DC

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft)**

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for taking comment before introduction. Frontier AI is the hardest policy problem this Congress faces, and your draft treats it seriously. We are writing to be equally serious about where it falls short.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers working for binding limits on frontier AI. In March 2025 we filed comments on the Office of Science and Technology Policy's AI Action Plan request for information, asking then for binding pre-deployment testing of frontier systems, protection for the states' right to act, and whistleblower protections. We write in the same spirit, in the same plain language our members use.

Our bottom line: we oppose the bill as drafted. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium — an immediate pause on training the most powerful systems until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled, together with a wind-down of the most powerful systems already in the world.

## Where we agree with the draft

The draft concedes the central point of this debate: that a line exists above which ordinary rules do not suffice. Section 101 draws that line at 10^26 computing operations — the draft's own definition of a "frontier model" — and builds a special set of duties around it. We agree with the line. The disagreement is about what follows from it. The draft asks developers above the line to describe what they are doing. We ask them to stop, prove control, and only then proceed.

Several parts of the draft deserve to survive into any final bill, and we say so plainly. Section 113's whistleblower protections are strong, non-waivable and long overdue; we support them. Sections 131 and 132 raise penalties for AI-enabled fraud and for impersonating government officials; we support those. Title IV's testbeds and NAIRR codification build research capacity the country needs, and the Section 321 review of model-weight and open-source security addresses a real and neglected danger. None of that is at issue in our opposition.

## Why the core of the draft cannot carry the weight

The heart of the draft is Section 111 (transparency) and Section 112 (independent verification organization audits). Walk through what these sections actually require.

Section 111 tells large frontier developers to write, implement and publish their own "frontier AI framework" — their own plan for assessing catastrophic risk — within a year. All frontier developers must publish transparency reports, and the required contents are telling: the model's release date, the languages it supports, its output types, its intended use, and how to contact the developer. Critical safety incidents — stolen model weights, failed risk controls, loss of control of a model — are reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days, or within 24 hours to law enforcement only where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 112 then requires a licensed outside auditor, at least twice a year, to check whether the developer is following its own plan.

Every one of those duties lands after the fact. Reports describe incidents that have already happened. Audits check compliance with a plan the developer wrote itself. The draft's own definition of "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" (Section 101) is a balancing test — anticipated benefits outweighing catastrophic risks — which is a judgment call, not a demonstration of control. And nothing in either section slows, pauses or stops a single training run. A developer could comply with Sections 111 and 112 completely and still build and release a system that no one, including its maker, can control.

That is the whole of our objection. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory, and this draft leaves the trajectory untouched.

The draft's enforcement design confirms this. Violations of Section 111 carry civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day counted separately (Section 111(i)) — a cost of doing business for developers whose frontier training runs already cost hundreds of millions of dollars, and are on their way past a billion. There is no criminal liability anywhere in the frontier provisions, for anyone. CAISI, codified in Section 102 at $100 million a year, is directed to write voluntary guidelines, run evaluations and license auditors. Advice is not enforcement. We support CAISI in one role only: as the enforcement body for a moratorium.

Nor is the draft an outlier; it is the latest in a series of voluntary arrangements. The Administration's June executive order rests on reviews that developers may simply skip, with a thirty-day government look at new systems before release. The through-line of federal AI policy is "ask nicely." A bill that finally puts duties in statute should not stop at duties to describe.

## On Section 121, we ask you to strike it

Section 121 would block, for three years, any state law that specifically regulates the development of AI models. According to Rep. Trahan's office, it would federalize the frontier safety laws of California, New York and Illinois, and reach California's AB 2013 (training-data disclosure) and parts of SB 942 (AI transparency).

We oppose Section 121 outright, for three reasons.

First, the federal floor is weaker than what it replaces. Both regimes have a 24-hour clock for imminent dangers, but on the baseline New York's RAISE Act gives regulators 72 hours to hear about a critical safety incident, while the draft gives them 15 days. Preempting state law in order to impose slower reporting is not a national standard; it is a step backward.

Second, the freeze lands mid-stride. California's SB 53 has been in effect since January. New York's RAISE Act takes effect in January 2027. Illinois's SB 315 was signed in July. Section 121 would freeze all three for three years — and the federal obligations it substitutes sunset at the same three-year mark unless Congress reauthorizes them. If Congress fails to act on time, the country is left with neither the state laws nor the federal ones.

Third, the public has already weighed in. In our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters (fielded August 10–17; margin of error ±2.5 points), 63 percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Congress has been here before: last year the Senate stripped a ten-year state-law moratorium from the reconciliation bill by a vote of 99 to 1. Preemption is the part of this debate Congress has already rejected once. Please do not revive it here.

## What we ask you to build instead

Replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a moratorium built on four parts.

**1. Pause.** An immediate halt on training any model above 10^26 computing operations — the draft's own line — until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Certification means a developer can show control before it builds, not describe its risks after.

**2. Wind down.** Frontier models already deployed that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — whose weights, once downloaded, cannot be recalled. U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them. The largest open-weight releases of 2026 came from Chinese labs; a pause that stops at our border would not protect Americans, and ours does not.

**3. Personal criminal liability.** Executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause face criminal penalties. In our August survey, 66 percent of voters said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. Civil fines alone will not slow a race this profitable.

**4. CAISI as the enforcement body.** CAISI should license independent testers, run certification, verify the wind-down, and refer violations for prosecution. We do not oppose its funding — its current appropriation is roughly $10 million a year, so the draft's $100 million is a real upgrade — but we support it only in that role.

## The FRONTIER Act

We understand the frontier-governance provisions of this draft have now been introduced separately as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, before the Energy and Commerce Committee. Everything in this letter applies to that bill with equal force. We would welcome the chance to work with the Committee as it takes up that legislation.

## Closing

Some will read this letter as asking Congress to do something radical. It is not. In June, Anthropic — a company building frontier systems — said publicly that "it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause" frontier development, because systems that can build their own successors may put human control at risk. When developers themselves ask for the option to stop, the only question is whether the pause comes by design or after a disaster. In our August survey, 74 percent said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, 52 percent are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival, and 49 percent support a temporary halt outright. The public is not the obstacle. The draft, as written, is not yet equal to the public.

We would welcome the chance to meet with your staff, to share our full survey toplines and crosstabs, and to connect you with our members — parents, nurses, machinists, pastors and researchers — who live with the stakes of this decision every day. Thank you for the genuinely bipartisan effort this draft represents. We would rather argue with you about how to stop the race than about whether to.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

# Hill one-pager — Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft

*For Energy & Commerce member offices — Frontier Restraint Coalition, October 2026. Draft for Executive Director sign-off.*

---

## Stop the race, then set the rules: replace GAAIA's reporting regime with a frontier pause

**What's happening.** Reps. Obernolte (R-CA) and Trahan (D-MA) released a 269-page discussion draft on June 4 to create the first federal framework for frontier AI. The frontier-governance provisions are also before E&C as the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925); committee action is possible this fall.

**The problem.** The draft's core is transparency and reporting. Section 111 asks large developers to publish safety plans they write themselves and report incidents after they happen; Section 112 hires outside auditors to check whether companies followed their own plans. Nothing in the bill slows a single training run. No developer can show its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does. Section 121 would block state AI safety laws — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois's SB 315 — for three years, for a federal floor that is weaker in places (15-day vs. 72-hour incident reporting).

## Our asks

1. **Pause, don't just report.** Replace the frontier-developer provisions (Secs. 111–112) with an immediate pause on training above 10^26 computing operations — the draft's own "frontier model" line — until Congress certifies these systems can be reliably controlled.
2. **Wind down what's already out.** Deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months — including open-weight releases (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen), whose weights cannot be recalled once downloaded. U.S. cloud providers stop serving them.
3. **Personal accountability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause.
4. **Strike Sec. 121 preemption.** Let California, New York and Illinois keep the laws they have already enacted.
5. **Keep the good parts.** Whistleblower protections (Sec. 113), AI-fraud penalties (Secs. 131–132), research capacity (Title IV) — and repurpose CAISI (Sec. 102) as the moratorium's enforcement body, not a voluntary standards shop.

**By the numbers** (FRC national survey, Aug 2026; n=1,512 registered voters; ±2.5 pts): 74% want Congress to require companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. 63% say federal law should not block state AI safety laws. 66% support criminal penalties for mass harm. 49% support a temporary halt to training the most powerful systems.

**Bottom line.** There is no safe path on the current trajectory. A reporting regime that leaves the race intact leaves the threat intact.

**Contact:** Frontier Restraint Coalition policy team — [contact to be added by comms before distribution].

# Staff Q&A — anticipated questions on FRC's GAAIA position

*Prep for Hill meetings, keyed to the four questions in the 2 Oct briefing. Answers ≤120 words each. Positions per messaging guide v4; facts checked 16 Oct 2026. Draft for Executive Director sign-off — speaker notes, not for distribution.*

---

**1. "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"** *(Majority E&C staff)*

Every duty in the draft lands after the fact. Reporting describes incidents that have already happened. Audits check whether a company followed its own plan. The draft's own definition of "acceptable" risk mitigation is a benefits-versus-risks judgment call, not proof of control. And nothing in the bill slows a single training run. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat: no developer can show its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does. Even Anthropic said in June the world needs the option to pause. CAISI as drafted writes voluntary guidelines — we support it only as the moratorium's enforcement arm.

---

**2. "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"** *(Minority staff, Trahan-aligned)*

Dropping preemption would fix one serious flaw, and we'd give a revised text a fresh look. But our opposition doesn't rest on preemption alone: transparency and reporting are not restraint, and without a pause the race — and the threat — stays fully intact. On preemption itself, we oppose it at any length. Three years would freeze California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois's SB 315 mid-phase-in, for a federal floor that is weaker in places: 15-day incident reporting instead of New York's 72 hours. Sixty-three percent of voters say federal law should not block state AI safety laws. The sponsors narrowed preemption in H.R. 9925; we still oppose it there.

---

**3. "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"** *(Senate Commerce staff)*

The race already includes China — the open-weight frontier is now largely set there. The largest open releases of 2026 came from Chinese labs: Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4, GLM-5.2, Qwen 3.8. That is exactly why our moratorium doesn't stop at the border: uncertified open-weight models would be wound down in the U.S., and American cloud providers would stop serving them. The competitiveness argument also assumes the race can be run safely. No developer — American or Chinese — can show that. Losing a capability race is recoverable; losing control of frontier systems may not be. The country that certifies control before it builds sets the standard everyone else has to meet.

---

**4. "CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"** *(Appropriations staff)*

$100 million a year for FY2027–29 is a real increase over the roughly $10 million CAISI received in FY2026, and the fee authority is sensible. But the level matters less than the authorities. As drafted, CAISI writes voluntary guidelines, runs evaluations and licenses auditors; it cannot stop anything, and developers can decline its advice. We support CAISI in one role: the enforcement body for a frontier moratorium — licensing independent testers, running certification, verifying the wind-down, and referring violations for prosecution. If the sponsors keep it advisory, no funding level makes it adequate. Worth noting: the House Science version advanced in June authorizes only $20 million a year, so the number is still unsettled.

---
